extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century periodical readers; readers of essays, theatre news, and social commentary
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and newsy commentary from an early-18th-century periodical offering theatrical criticism, social observation, and rhetorical advice. The content mixes theatre review, moral exempla, and conversational anecdote aimed at general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic effect: incidents over fine language
rubrics_metrics.description: The soul is not to be moved by words, but things; for the incidents in this drama are laid together so happily, that the spectator makes the play for himself, by the force which the circumstance has upon his imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play's emotional power rests on its incidents and circumstances rather than on elegant lines. Even with dry or inelegant expression, well-arranged incidents can move an audience—though this effect may fail for viewers who over-analyze and examine 'why they are pleased.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor's person and behaviour as part of success
rubrics_metrics.description: The person and behaviour of Mr. Wilks has no small share in conducing to the popularity of the play; and when a handsome fellow is going to a more coarse exit than beheading, his shape and countenance make every tender one reprieve him...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance, physical appearance, and stage presence materially affect audience sympathy and the popularity of a production; an actor's looks and comportment can create emotional responses independent of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy genius: discernment of spirit and unifying motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's great address in showing covetousness the motive of the actions of the Puritan, the epicure, the gamester, and the trader... shows he had to a great perfection, that discernment of spirit, which constitutes a genius for comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibiting a single underlying human vice (here, covetousness) as the common motive across diverse character types demonstrates the playwright's insight and constitutes a hallmark of great comic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witty device — 'the bite' (bantering/decoying witticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A Biter is one who tells you a thing you have no reason to disbelieve in itself; and perhaps has given you, before he bit you, no reason to disbelieve it for his saying it; and if you give him credit, laughs in your face, and triumphs that he has deceived you.' Also described as asking a bantering question or telling a damned lie in a serious manner, then revealing the 'bite.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To perform a successful 'bite', present a plausible statement or question in earnest so the target accepts it, then expose the deception to provoke amusement; it is a courtly/upper-class refinement of wit but depends on treating the target as credulous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial virtue: impartiality and legal wisdom (Verus model)
rubrics_metrics.description: He considered justice as a cardinal virtue, not as a trade for maintenance... The prisoner knew, that though his spirit was broken with guilt, and incapable of language to defend itself, all would be gathered from him which could conduce to his safety; and that his judge would wrest no law to destroy him, nor conceal any that could save him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good judge should be learned in law, impartial, treat justice as a moral duty rather than a means of livelihood, avoid abusing legal power, and actively seek to ensure fairness and the prisoner's safety where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness vs. affectedness in social presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frank Careless... goes to his glass, sets his wig awry, tumbles his cravat; and in short, undresses himself to go into company. Will Nice is so little satisfied with his dress, that all the time he is at a visit, he is still mending it... for he who studies carelessness, has, at least, his work the sooner done of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic seeming carelessness (naturalness) is preferable to visibly studied affectation; affectation of style or behaviour is more insufferable than genuine casualness. This observation functions as social criticism and as an implicit standard for credible character portrayal in literature and theatre.
